about.intro_content: Prof. Bin-Kui Li is Director of the Department of Liver Surgery at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC), Guangzhou. He treats hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) as part of a multidisciplinary liver cancer team.
about.detailed_content: Prof. Li has co-authored numerous peer-reviewed studies on hepatocellular carcinoma prognosis and treatment, including work on liver function assessment tools such as the modified albumin-bilirubin (mALBI) grade, and molecular prognostic markers including microRNA-106b. His research has also examined surgical outcomes for liver metastases, including partial hepatectomy for liver metastases originating from nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

faq.section_heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Prof. Bin-Kui Li

items.question: Does Prof. Bin-Kui Li accept international patients?
items.answer: CancerFax can coordinate medical report review and consultation support for international patients seeking an opinion related to liver cancer at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, subject to hospital availability and case acceptance.

items.question: What is Prof. Li's area of specialisation?
items.answer: Prof. Li specialises in the surgical and multidisciplinary treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma, with a research focus on liver function assessment and prognostic markers.

items.question: How can I request a consultation or second opinion?
items.answer: Submit your medical reports through CancerFax. The CancerFax team reviews the documents, prepares the case for submission, and coordinates next steps with SYSUCC's International Medical Center, subject to availability.

items.question: Does Prof. Li's team assess liver function before treatment?
items.answer: Yes. Prof. Li has contributed to refining liver function grading tools such as the modified albumin-bilirubin (mALBI) grade, which helps guide individualised treatment planning for hepatocellular carcinoma.

items.question: Does Prof. Li treat liver metastases from other cancers?
items.answer: Yes. Prof. Li has published research on surgical outcomes for liver metastases, including cases originating from nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
